title: I'm Really Good at Multitasking, Miss!
author: Thahmina Begum
summary: Thahmina Begum, writing in a bi-weekly teaching-and-learning bulletin, dismantles the common student claim of being good at multitasking, using Doug Lemov's Reconnect and cognitive load theory to argue that divided attention is simply reduced-quality task switching, made worse in adolescents by a prefrontal cortex that isn't fully developed until 25. Even with her school's existing phone ban and structured routines (SLANT for attention, SLOP for extended practice), she argues these mechanisms aren't precise enough to counter what she calls the insidious effects of habituated digital task-switching, and zeroes in on one specific, high-frequency classroom error: allowing students to write while the teacher is talking. She names this explicitly as the redundancy effect from cognitive load theory - a student trying to listen and transcribe simultaneously overloads working memory and effectively processes neither well - and notes that well-intentioned sins of enthusiasm (wanting to capture the teacher's words) make the error harder to spot and correct than outright disengagement. Her proposed fix is procedural rather than just aspirational: front-load the expectation with a specific reason, allow visible take-up time when calling for full attention, and consistently follow through when students slip, treating attention management as a trainable classroom habit rather than a one-off instruction.
points: Begum opens by knocking down the premise students often assert ("I'm good at multitasking"), grounding the rebuttal in Lemov's Reconnect and the neuroscience of an underdeveloped prefrontal cortex in adolescents.

She identifies allowing students to write while you speak as the single most common attention-fracturing error she sees, naming it explicitly as the redundancy effect from cognitive load theory rather than just a vague classroom-management issue.

Begum credits her school's existing phone ban and SLANT/SLOP routines as necessary but insufficient on their own, arguing teachers need to be much more precise about small-scale attention slips within lessons that already look orderly.

Her three-step enforcement routine (front-load the expectation, allow take-up time, follow through) turns "don't write while I'm talking" from a one-off reminder into a specific, repeatable classroom procedure.
quotes: No. No you’re not. Multitasking is merely task switching and each task is being completed slightly less effectively than if you were attending to them, one at a time.
In Lemov’s ‘Reconnect’, we learn that ‘the prefrontal cortex – the region of the brain that exerts impulse control and self discipline – isn’t fully developed until aged 25.
At first, our phones fracture our attention when we use them, but after a time our minds are rewired for distraction. Soon enough our phones are within us.

If students are writing as well as listening, it is highly likely they are overloading their working memory and will not process effectively what is being said (or written) - this is known as the redundancy effect, part of cognitive load theory.

Often, students are eager to get down your words of gold and so will not heed your instruction to SLANT. Lemov calls this ‘sins of enthusiasm’, which I love, but however well intentioned it is, we must direct their attention accordingly.
This week then, fight the attention fracturing phone effect with your high expectations in the classroom: do not allow students to write or speak when you are addressing them.
